title: Data Structures & Algorithms
description: The structures behind Java collections, their costs, and the algorithms interviews ask about.
resumo: Big-O: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²). A lookup inside a loop multiplies.
ArrayList: O(1) by index and at the end, O(n) in the middle and for `contains`. The default list.
LinkedList: O(1) at the ends, O(n) by index — rarely faster than ArrayList; use ArrayDeque for both ends.
Stack (LIFO) and queue (FIFO): `ArrayDeque` with `push/pop` or `offer/poll`, never `java.util.Stack`.
HashMap / HashSet: O(1) average by key; order is not guaranteed — LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when it matters.
TreeMap / TreeSet: sorted, O(log n), with ceiling/floor navigation; the comparator defines equality.
Binary search: O(log n), only on sorted data.
Sorting is O(n log n) and stable for objects; build comparators with `Comparator.comparing`, never by subtraction.
Recursion needs a base case; each call is a stack frame — use a loop for deep or linear data.

subsections.subtitle: Big-O Notation
subsections.description: How cost grows with the size of the input.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** code that is instant with 100 records takes minutes with a million, and nobody saw it coming in code review.

**Concept:** Big-O describes how the work grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constants. O(1): constant, independent of n (reading `array[i]`). O(log n): halves the problem each step (binary search). O(n): one pass over the data. O(n log n): efficient sorting. O(n²): a loop inside a loop over the same data. Space complexity measures extra memory the same way.

**How it works:** count the loops over the input and what each step costs. A method call inside a loop counts too: `list.contains(x)` on an `ArrayList` is O(n), so calling it inside a loop is O(n²).
examples.interview_question: What is Big-O notation, and what is the complexity of a nested loop over the same list?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Hidden O(n²): a linear lookup inside a loop. `List.contains` scans the whole list, so checking each element of one list against another is quadratic. A `HashSet` makes each lookup O(1).

subsections.subtitle: Arrays and ArrayList
subsections.description: Contiguous storage: fast by index, slow in the middle.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you need to keep a sequence of items, read them by position and add more as they arrive.

**Concept:** an array stores elements side by side in memory, so reading by index is O(1). Its size is fixed. `ArrayList` wraps an array and grows it automatically: when it is full, it allocates a bigger one (about 1.5×) and copies the elements, so adding at the end is O(1) amortized. Inserting or removing in the middle shifts every element after it: O(n).

**How it works:** `ArrayList` is the default list in Java. If you know the final size, pass it to the constructor to avoid repeated copying.
examples.code:
List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(1_000);   // capacity known: no resizing
items.add("book");          // O(1) amortized, at the end
items.get(0);               // O(1), by index
items.add(0, "pen");        // O(n): shifts every element right
items.remove(0);            // O(n): shifts every element left
items.contains("book");     // O(n): scans the list
examples.interview_question: What are the costs of add, get and insert in the middle of an ArrayList, and why?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Calling `remove(1)` on a `List<Integer>`. It removes the element at index 1, not the value 1 — `remove(int)` is chosen over `remove(Object)`. Box the value to remove by value.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you read that linked lists insert in O(1) and switch an `ArrayList` to `LinkedList` "for performance" — and it gets slower.

**Concept:** a linked list stores each element in a node that points to the next (and, in Java's `LinkedList`, the previous). Adding or removing at either end is O(1), and so is removing through an iterator you already hold. But reaching position i means walking i nodes: `get(i)` is O(n). Nodes are scattered in memory, so iterating is also slower in practice than over an array.

**How it works:** in real code, `ArrayList` is almost always faster. For adding and removing at both ends, use `ArrayDeque`.
examples.interview_question: When is a LinkedList better than an ArrayList?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Looping over a `LinkedList` with `get(i)`. Each call walks from the start, so the loop becomes O(n²). Iterate with for-each (or an iterator).

subsections.subtitle: Stacks and Queues
subsections.description: Last in first out, and first in first out.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** undo history, matching brackets, processing tasks in arrival order — they all need items taken out in a specific order.

**Concept:** a stack is LIFO (last in, first out): `push` adds on top and `pop` removes from the top. A queue is FIFO (first in, first out): `offer` adds at the end and `poll` removes from the front. All operations are O(1). In Java, `ArrayDeque` implements both through the `Deque` interface; the old `Stack` class extends the synchronized `Vector` and should not be used.

**How it works:** declare the variable as `Deque<T>` and use one consistent set of methods for the role you need.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue, and which Java class do you use for each?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Mixing `Deque` methods from different roles. `push` adds to the front, but `add` adds to the end; adding with `add` and taking with `pop` makes your "stack" behave like a queue.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** finding a user by email in a list of a million users means scanning the list every time.

**Concept:** a hash table computes a hash code from the key and uses it to choose a bucket in an internal array, so lookup, insert and removal are O(1) on average. Two keys can land in the same bucket (a collision); `equals` then tells them apart. That is why keys must implement `hashCode` and `equals` consistently. `HashSet` is a `HashMap` with only keys.

**How it works:** use `HashMap` whenever you look things up by key and do not need order; `LinkedHashMap` keeps insertion order, and `TreeMap` keeps keys sorted.
examples.interview_question: How does a HashMap find a value in O(1), and why do keys need equals and hashCode?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Relying on the iteration order of a `HashMap`. The order depends on hash codes and capacity, is not guaranteed, and can change between JDK versions or as the map grows — so output and tests change "by themselves". Use `LinkedHashMap` (insertion order) or `TreeMap` (sorted).

subsections.subtitle: Trees and TreeMap
subsections.description: Sorted data with O(log n) operations.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you need the data sorted at all times — the next appointment after 14:00, the products in a price range — not only fast lookups.

**Concept:** a binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so a search goes down one path. If the tree stays balanced, its height is about log₂ n, and search, insert and delete are O(log n). Java's `TreeMap` and `TreeSet` are red-black trees (self-balancing) and keep keys sorted, with navigation methods such as `floorKey`, `ceilingKey`, `headMap` and `subMap`.

**How it works:** the keys must be `Comparable`, or you pass a `Comparator` to the constructor.
examples.interview_question: When would you use a TreeMap instead of a HashMap?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A `Comparator` that compares only part of the object. `TreeSet` considers two elements equal when the comparator returns 0, so two different people with the same name silently become one.

subsections.subtitle: Searching: Linear and Binary Search
subsections.description: Finding an element in O(n) or O(log n).

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** checking whether a value exists in a sorted list of a million entries by looking at every one.

**Concept:** linear search checks each element in turn: O(n), and it works on any list. Binary search needs a sorted list: look at the middle, discard the half that cannot contain the value, repeat — O(log n), about 20 steps for a million elements. In Java, `Collections.binarySearch` and `Arrays.binarySearch` do it; they return the index, or a negative number if the value is absent.

**How it works:** sort once (O(n log n)) when you will search many times; for a single search, linear is cheaper.
examples.interview_question: How does binary search work, and what does it require?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Binary search on an unsorted list. It does not fail — it silently returns a wrong answer, usually "not found" for a value that is there.

subsections.subtitle: Sorting
subsections.description: O(n log n) sorting and comparators.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** orders must be listed by date, then by total; customers by name, ignoring case.

**Concept:** efficient general-purpose sorts are O(n log n). Java sorts objects with TimSort, which is stable — elements that compare equal keep their original order — and fast on data that is already partly sorted. You rarely write a sort yourself: you write a `Comparator` that says how two elements compare, and call `List.sort` or `Stream.sorted`.

**How it works:** build comparators with `Comparator.comparing`, `thenComparing` and `reversed()`; they read like the business rule.
examples.interview_question: What is the complexity of sorting in Java, and what does "stable" mean?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A comparator written as a subtraction. `a.age() - b.age()` overflows for large or negative values and returns the wrong sign, so the sort silently breaks. Use `Integer.compare` or `Comparator.comparingInt`.

subsections.subtitle: Recursion
subsections.description: A function that solves a problem by calling itself.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** some problems are naturally nested: categories inside categories, folders inside folders, a JSON tree.

**Concept:** a recursive method solves a small case directly (the base case) and reduces every other case to a smaller version of the same problem. Each call takes a frame on the thread's stack until it returns, so the depth of the recursion costs memory, and without a base case it never stops (`StackOverflowError`).

**How it works:** write the base case first, make sure every call moves toward it, and prefer a loop when the depth can be large.
examples.interview_question: What are the parts of a recursive function, and what can go wrong with deep recursion?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Recursing over long linear data, one call per element. A list of 100,000 nodes means 100,000 stack frames, and the thread's stack overflows. Java does not optimize tail calls — use a loop.
